d: The final maturation of sperm in the female tract. It removes cholesterol and glycoproteins from the sperm membrane, so the sperm can bind the zona pellucida and undergo the acrosome reaction.
The outer, multinucleated trophoblast layer. It invades the endometrium, opens maternal vessels and secretes hCG and human placental lactogen, and it covers every chorionic villus.
The thickened endometrium beneath the implantation site, which forms the maternal part of the placenta. If it is deficient, villi attach directly to the myometrium, as in placenta accreta.
A syncytiotrophoblast hormone, also called human chorionic somatomammotropin. It causes maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis, so glucose and amino acids are spared for the fetus.
Unbalanced blood flow through vessel connections in a shared monochorionic placenta. The donor twin becomes anemic with oligohydramnios, and the recipient becomes polycythemic with polyhydramnios.

Cells from the crest of the folding neural plate that migrate through the embryo. They form peripheral ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, the adrenal medulla, enteric ganglia, skull and facial bones, and the aorticopulmonary septum. Failed migration causes Hirschsprung disease.
Fingerlike projections of the chorion, covered by syncytiotrophoblast, that carry fetal capillaries into the intervillous space. They are the fetal half of the placenta.
The number of chorions, and so of placentas, that twins share. Ultrasound reads it in the first trimester, and a monochorionic placenta allows the vessel connections that cause twin-twin transfusion.
